title: The daily office
hook: Anglicans pray the Book of Common Prayer morning and evening, with short set prayers called collects

segments.voice: Yesterday, the icon, and your line: a window, not a wall. Did a photo turn into a window for you? Today, prayers with a timetable. Day one hundred seven.

Five thirty on a weekday in an English cathedral. Outside, traffic and buses. Inside, a choir in robes, a dozen people in the old wooden seats, and the same service that has been sung there, in some form, for centuries. It's called Evensong. It goes back to 1549, when Thomas Cranmer, the Archbishop of Canterbury, took the church's daily prayers, which were in Latin and spread across seven services meant for monks, and put them into English, in two: one for morning, one for evening. He called his book the Book of Common Prayer. Common, as in shared. Anyone could pray it, at home or in church. And tucked into both services are tiny prayers, a single sentence each. Today's word is their name.

A collect. Say it with the stress at the front: COLL-ect. It's a short set prayer with a shape. It speaks to God, often recalls something about God, asks for one thing, and closes through Christ. One breath, one request. Nobody is quite sure where the name comes from. One old idea is that it collects the silent prayers of everyone present into one sentence. The whole rhythm is called the daily office, from the Latin for duty or service. It's older than any church: the Psalms speak of praying "Evening, and morning, and at noon," and Daniel prayed three times a day. Now the most famous collect of all, near the end of Evening Prayer, is the one for aid against all perils. Cranmer translated it from an old Latin night prayer. In the 1662 Book of Common Prayer: "Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night; for the love of thy only Son, our Saviour, Jesus Christ. Amen." Picture the world it was written for. No streetlights. Night meant real danger: fire, illness, thieves, the dark itself. People said it before bed, and many still do. Anglicans pray it; so do many Episcopalians and Methodists. Catholics keep their own daily office, the Liturgy of the Hours, and the Orthodox pray Vespers at evening and Matins at morning. Different books, the same idea: time itself, marked with prayer, morning and evening, like a heartbeat.
screen: `A COLLECT: ONE BREATH, ONE REQUEST.` · `EVENING, AND MORNING, AND AT NOON.` · `AID AGAINST ALL PERILS.` · then, large: `LIGHTEN OUR DARKNESS.` · then: `TIME MARKED LIKE A HEARTBEAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray the evening collect, or simply hear it. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say it slowly, out loud or under your breath: Lighten our darkness, we beseech thee, O Lord; and by thy great mercy defend us from all perils and dangers of this night. If you don't pray, just let the words pass through you, and notice which phrase stays. Then think of one darkness, yours or someone else's, that could use some light tonight. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
screen: `LIGHTEN OUR DARKNESS, WE BESEECH THEE, O LORD.`

segments.voice: Collect. A short set prayer of one sentence, prayed morning and evening in the Book of Common Prayer. Stress at the front: COLL-ect. Today's word.
Your line: lighten our darkness. Tonight, when you turn off the last light, say those three words, or just remember them. Day one hundred seven.

howItsDone: Many Anglicans and Episcopalians pray Morning and Evening Prayer from the Book of Common Prayer, at home or in church, ending with set collects; cathedrals often sing Evensong daily, and Catholics and Orthodox Christians keep their own daily hours of prayer.

fork.setup: you're Thomas Cranmer in 1549. the church's daily prayers are in Latin, spread over seven services made for monks. what do you do?
options: put them into English, in a morning and an evening service.
fork.reveal: he made two services in English, Morning and Evening Prayer, so anyone could pray them. the name says it: common prayer.

original.note: Latin: a gathering. one old explanation says the collect gathers everyone's prayers into one.

trapdoor: what you thought: collect means to gather things up.
what it means: COLL-ect, a one-sentence set prayer, like "lighten our darkness," prayed morning and evening.
what a scholar hears: the origin of the name is uncertain; the Latin collecta may mean the prayer that gathers the people's prayers. Cranmer translated many collects from older Latin prayers.

notes: The 'aid against all perils' collect is generally traced to a Latin Compline collect (Illumina, quaesumus, Domine, tenebras nostras) in the Sarum use. Stated only as 'an old Latin night prayer'. Confirm.
Cranmer's two offices drew on the monastic hours (Matins, Lauds, Prime; Vespers, Compline); 'seven services into two' simplifies (eight hours are sometimes counted). Confirm phrasing.
Origin of the word 'collect' presented as uncertain, with the 'gathering the people's prayers' explanation as one old idea. Confirm.
Evensong 'for centuries': the BCP services were banned during the Commonwealth (1640s–1660), so the phrasing avoids claiming an unbroken run.
The practice repeats a real BCP prayer (not a new prayer). The Methodist mention: Wesley's Sunday Service drew on the BCP; confirm 'many Methodists' is fair.
